, entanglement of an arbitrary
number of qubits can be generated in a single operation. This property has many
potential applications, and may specifically enable an accelerated implementation
of certain quantum error correction codes. In this work, we look at the
fault-tolerant feasibility of the linear cluster state, which is one of the
most well-studied quantum error correction codes in the many-qubit setting.
Using the model of faulty quantum circuit logic, we show that two faulty
generation of entangled qubit pairs, coupled with faulty cluster state
measurements, is sufficient to cause a failure in the fault-tolerant
implementation of the linear cluster state. This result contrasts with the
fault-tolerant generation of GHZ states, which requires three faulty
generation operations. We discuss the practical implications of our results,
and argue that the linear cluster state may be particularly challenging to
implement fault-tolerantly in any QC architecture that is capable of
entangling an arbitrary number of qubits.
  We also introduce the concept of a "fault-tolerant threshold" for a particular
quantum error correction code and QC architecture, and provide an analytical
expression for this threshold in the case of the linear cluster state and
quantum circuit logic. Our results provide a new and practical way to compare
the fault-tolerant robustness of different QC codes and architectures.
  Finally, we provide a set of guidelines for implementing the linear cluster
state fault-tolerantly, and provide specific remedies for preventing logical
cluster state decoherence in two particular QC architectures under study.
Specifically, we show that the need for faulty cluster state measurements can
be completely avoided if the qubits in the cluster are decoded before any
faults manifest themselves, and that the likelihood of faulty generation
operations can be made arbitrarily small in an experimental setup where the
fidelity of the entangling gate can be made arbitrarily close to unity.
  In summary, this work provides a detailed study of the fault-tolerant
feasibility of one particular quantum error correction code (the linear cluster
state) in an architecture (quantum circuit logic) where many-qubit entanglement
can be generated in a single operation. We hope that our results will be
useful in guiding the experimental implementation of any cluster state-based
quantum error correction code.

literature, as the major medium that carries knowledge between scientists,
exhibits explosive growth during the last century. Despite the frequent use of
many tangible measures, such as citation, impact factor and g-index, to
quantify the influence of papers from different perspectives based on
scientific productivity, it has not yet been well understood how the
relationship between scientific productivity and knowledge amount turns out to
be, i.e., how the knowledge value of papers and knowledge amount vary with
development of the discipline. This raises the question of whether high
scientific productivity equals large knowledge amount. Here, building on rich
literature on academic conferences and journals, we collect 185 million
articles covering 19 disciplines published during 1970 to 2020, and establish
citation network research area to represent the knowledge flow from the authors
of the article being cited to the authors of the articles that cite it under
each specific area. As a result, the structure formed during the evolution of
each scientific area can implicitly tells how the knowledge flows between nodes
and how it behaves as the number of literature (productivity) increases. By
leveraging Structural entropy in structured high-dimensional space and Shannon
entropy in unstructured probability space, we propose the Quantitative Index of
Knowledge (KQI), which is taken as the subtraction between the two types of
entropy, to reflect the extent of disorder of the structure of article network
in each field. A set of experiments are conducted based on different types of
entropy and their combinations, which shows that the final result is not
dependent on the choice of function. And the analysis on the article list with
the highest knowledge value indicates that the knowledge value of each article
is not absolute and has different significance in different areas. Our study
shows that the understanding of scientific productivity and knowledge amount is
insufficient, and the essential connection between the two is represented by
quantitative index of knowledge. The research on scientific knowledge amount
could provide new insights into evaluating the knowledge generated by human
beings, which may promote the growth of global knowledge.

is shown to have a dependence on the spin-orbit coupling, which is able to

of viscoelasticity on helical propulsion is controlled by a snowman-like
effect, previously reported for dumbbell swimmers, wherein the front-back
asymmetry of the swimmer leads to a non-Newtonian elastic force that can either
favor or hinder locomotion.
  Our results are such that even the same swimmer design can exhibit either a
significant increase, decrease or no change in speed when immersed in the
viscoelastic fluid. This lead us to propose a simple index based on a
dimensionless ratio of the helical tail and body sizes which predicts the
behavior of the speed in the viscoelastic fluid. This index also reproduces
exactly the results obtained in Newtonian fluids, indicating that the effect of
viscoelasticity is controlled solely on a scaling level. Such a result could be
useful to estimate the impact of viscoelasticity in other helical swimming
contexts.

non-equilibrium elastic effect that results in a permanent deformation of the
helical tail that leads to larger locomotory displacements, while the decrease
can be attributed to an equilibrium elastic effect that hinders locomotion.
Overall, our work underlines the importance of considering the geometry of
helical swimmers in viscoelastic fluids.

real biologcal systems, such as the mussels, that are attached to walls in
viscoelastic fluids. It could also be useful to design optimal helical

minate through droplets ejected by
infected individuals during coughing, sneezing, speaking and breathing. The
spread of the infection and hence its menace depend on how the virus-loaded
droplets evolve in space and time with changing environmental conditions. In
view of this, we investigate the evolution of the droplets within the purview
of the Brownian motion of the evaporating droplets in the air with varying
weather conditions under the action of gravity. We track the movement of the
droplets till either they gravitationally settle on the ground or evaporate to
aerosols of size 2$\mu$m or less. Droplets with radii $2 \mu$m or less may
continue to diffuse and remain suspended in the air for long time. The effects
of relative humidity and temperature on the evaporation are found to be
significant. We note that under strong flowing conditions droplets travel large
distances. It is found that the bigger droplets fall on the ground due to the
dominance of gravity over the diffusive force despite the loss of mass due to
evaporation. The smaller evaporating droplets may not settle on the ground but
remain suspended in the air due to the dominance of the diffusive force. The
fate of the intermediate size droplets depends on the weather conditions and
play crucial roles in the spread of the infection. These environment dependent
effects may be important in the context of COVID19 infection and may be valid
for other respiratory infections.
  We present the probability distributions of the droplets for different
weather conditions in graphical as well as tabular forms. The results may be
important in the context of COVID19 infection and may be valid for other
respiratory infections.
  Finally, we discuss the results in the perspective of COVID19 infection and
find that the intermediate size droplets play crucial roles in the spread of
infection. It may be the most important and least talked aspect of the droplet
diffusion and evaporation in space and time with changing environmental
conditions.
  The present work may be useful to the researchers to develop models of
airborne transmission, and to evaluate the risk of infection, determine the
need for and effectiveness of personal protective equipment, and develop
strategies for disease control.
  It may be noted that the present work does not aim at any mathematical
analysis of the COVID19 infection, rather it talks of the droplets which are
known to disseminate the infection.

NN-based inference is more complicated than in traditional methods. This is
because in addition to aleatoric uncertainty associated with noisy data, there
is also uncertainty due to limited data, but also due to NN hyperparameters,
overparametrization, optimization and sampling errors as well as model
misspecification. Although there are some recent works on uncertainty
quantification (UQ) in NNs, there is no systematic investigation of suitable
methods towards quantifying the total uncertainty effectively and efficiently
even for function approximation, and there is even less work on solving partial
differential equations and learning operator mappings between
infinite-dimensional function spaces using NNs. In this work, we present a
comprehensive framework that includes uncertainty modeling, new and existing
solution methods, as well as evaluation metrics and post-hoc improvement
approaches. To demonstrate the applicability and reliability of our framework,
we present an extensive comparative study in which various methods are tested
on prototype problems, including problems with mixed input-output data, and
stochastic problems in high dimensions. In the Appendix, we include a
comprehensive description of all the UQ methods employed, which we will make
available as a Python package. Our framework and study provide a basis for
developing new and efficient UQ methods in NNs and for evaluating their
performance.
  We present a comparative study of various methods for uncertainty
quantification (UQ) in neural networks (NNs). All methods are tested on a
carefully selected set of function approximation problems with different types
of data, including ransom sampling in high dimensions and physical data
generated by stochastic ordinary differential equations. The performance of the
methods is evaluated based on a priori error estimates, computational
costs and the ability to approximate total uncertainty, which is quantified
using a new uncertainty score. Besides comparing established methods, our
study also highlights the potential of improved post-hoc test metrics to
better capture the ability of a method to approximate the total uncertainty.
We present a Python package containing all methods and metrics, and provide a
clear description of each test case and all results.

) have become an established part of
numerous safety-critical computer vision applications, including human robot
interactions and automated driving. Real-world implementations will need to
guarantee their robustness against hardware soft errors corrupting the
underlying platform memory. Based on the previously observed efficacy of
activation clipping techniques, we build a prototypical safety case for
classifier CNNs by demonstrating that range supervision represents a highly
reliable fault detector and mitigator with respect to relevant bit flips,
adopting an eight-exponent floating point data representation. We further
explore novel, non-uniform range restriction methods that effectively suppress
the probability of silent data corruptions and uncorrectable errors. As a
safety-relevant end-to-end use case, we showcase the benefit of our approach in
a vehicle classification scenario, using ResNet-50 and the traffic camera data
set MIOVision. The quantitative evidence provided in this work can be leveraged
to inspire further and possibly more complex CNN safety arguments.
  We make our safety evidence quantitative by comparing it to a baseline CNN
implementation that uses unclipped floating point numbers. The analysis is
performed on a Bitlek Systems FPGACard board, using a Python-based Soft Error
Simulation framework, S3F. Our method demonstrates a 5,665x reduction in
silent data corruptions compared to the baseline, and a 1,022x reduction in
uncorrectable errors. Additionally, it achieves a higher than 99% accuracy in
classifying MIOVision images even after being subjected to various bit flips.
This high reliability holds across different activation representations and
precision levels, including sparsity-based and binary ones. It further remains
almost unaltered even after being stacked onto a general-purpose classifier. This
demonstrates that the benefit of static analysis techniques such as activation
clipping can extend to lower precision data representations in real-world
applications as well.

as defined in the glossaries of European
Central Bank, has a great impact on the economy of a country influencing the
exchanges and the interactions between companies. On short, netting refers to
an alternative to the usual way in which the companies make the payments to
each other: it is an agreement in which each party sets off amounts it owes
against amounts owed to it. Based on the amounts two or more parties owe
between them, the payment is substituted by a direct settlement. In this paper
we introduce a set of graph algorithms which provide optimal netting solutions
for the scale of a country economy. The set of algorithms computes results in
an efficient time and is tested on invoice data provided by the Romanian
Ministry of Economy. Our results show that classical graph algorithms are still
capable of solving very important modern problems.
  We introduce the following graph processing techniques in order to compute the
minimum amount of outstanding invoices: DFS (for computing cycles in an ergodic
graph), Dijkstra's algorithm (for computing the minimum netting cost for each
pair of companies) and a greedy algorithm (for computing the maximum netting
amount, which is equivalent to finding the largest cycles in an ergodic graph).
All the algorithms are tested on a large dataset, provided by the Romanian
Ministry of Economy, consisting in over 119 millions of invoices, representing
an approximate turnover of over 340 billion EUR. The testing results show that
our algorithms are capable of processing such large datasets in a reasonable
time and providing optimal netting solutions for a country economy.
  In conclusion, classical graph algorithms are still capable of solving very
important modern problems, which can have a major impact on the economy of a
country.
  Keywords: netting, outstanding invoices, minimum/maximum netting cost,
ergodic graph, cycle, DFS, Dijkstra's algorithm, greedy algorithm.

9, Chile, and especially its capital
city, Santiago, suffered from widespread violence with public and private
infrastructure destruction. This work aims to expand an epidemiological
non-local model that successfully described the French riots of 2005 to
incorporate the topology of Santiago's subway network and explain the reported
distribution of rioting activity in the city. Although the model reproduced the
disorders' aggregated temporal evolution, it could not deliver results
resembling the observed spatial distribution of activity on Santiago. The main
reason for this failure can be attributed to the fact that the model lacks a
population displacement mechanism, which seems vital to explain Santiago's
unrest episodes.
  A simple modification that incorporated non-local connections in a
individual-based model successfully reproduced the observed distribution of
rioting activity in Santiago. Moreover, this model did not require the
inclusion of the city's network topology to explain its distribution of
rioting activity.
  This work shows that rioting behavior in Chile's context cannot be explained
by the country's economic inequality, highlighting the importance of cultural
aspects that are still unquantified. Furthermore, the success of these models
Highlights the importance of including topology and population displacement as
integrative components to study civil unrest.
  Finally, this work delivers a novel approach to study Santiago's unrest by

matrix elements without assuming unitarity. We define two minimal sets of
experimental constraints -- direct $+$ inherent bounds and indirect bounds, and
analyze the implications of each set on leptonic non-unitarity. In addition, we
clarify the treatment of flux and cross-section predictions, taking into
account NP contamination in hadronic inputs. We use the currently running
FASER$\nu$ experiment as a case study in order to demonstrate the sensitivity
of collider neutrino experiments to leptonic non-unitarity. We find that
indirect bounds constrain LMM non-unitarity to below the $10^{-3}$ level,
stronger than current CKM non-unitarity constraints. Conversely, considering
only direct and inherent bounds we find that ${\cal O}(1)$ unitarity violation
is viable at $2\sigma$, and will be probed by the FASER$\nu$ experiment in the
current run of the LHC.
  Finally, we discuss future prospects in the presence of general extra
neutrino states, finding that $\sim 1$ event may be required to constrain
leptonic non-unitarity at the $\sigma$ level from collider data alone.

non-unitarity is below the $10^{-4}$ level.

Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms exploit the information from camera
and inertial sensors to estimate position and translation. Recent VIO models
employ deep neural networks to extract feature and pose information from
visual and inertial data, which need to be trained and integrated in a
coordinate system. However, existing VIO models are difficult to train since
(1) the visual and pose loss functions have different optimization targets and
scales, and (2) the training data are collected from two different streams:
visual and inertial. To address these issues, we propose a novel VIO model
which is trained with a single stream of raw images and pre-aligned
inertial data. To facilitate the training, we propose a novel joint visual
and pose loss function with a dual-optimization strategy. The model is
optimized by one-stage and two-stage ways to deal with the different
characteristics of visual and pose networks. Meanwhile, we propose two methods
to collect and augment the VIO training datasets. The experimental results
demonstrate that our model achieves better localization performance compared
to the state-of-the-art VIO models.
  We also conduct thorough module ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness
of each module in our model. Our code and data are released at
https://github.com/ShuZhaoLab/VIoT.

Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA). The goal of FedSA is to train a
student model for a new task with the help of several decentralized teachers,
whose pre-training tasks and data are different and agnostic. Our motivation
for investigating such a problem setup stems from a recent dilemma of model
sharing. Many researchers or institutes have spent enormous resources on
training large and competent networks. Due to the privacy, security, or
intellectual property issues, they are, however, not able to share their own
pre-trained models, even if they wish to contribute to the community. The
proposed FedSA offers a solution to this dilemma and makes it one step further
since, again, the learned student may specialize in a new task different from
all of the teachers. To this end, we proposed a dedicated strategy for handling
FedSA. Specifically, our student-training process is driven by a novel
saliency-based approach that adaptively selects teachers as the participants
and integrates their representative capabilities into the student. To evaluate
the effectiveness of FedSA, we conduct experiments on both single-task and
multi-task settings. Experimental results demonstrate that FedSA effectively
amalgamates knowledge from decentralized models and achieves competitive
performance to centralized baselines.
  Which tasks are FedSA good for? The answer depends on the diversity of the
teachers' tasks. If the teachers' tasks are diverse, FedSA is good for tasks
that are likely to be impossible for a single teacher to learn. Otherwise,
FedSA specializes in a few tasks similar to the teachers.

new insights into the characteristics of grid cells and their neural
neighborhood, the parahippocampal-hippocampal region, calling for a revision
and refinement of earlier grid cell models. This survey paper aims to provide a
comprehensive summary of grid cell research published in the past decade. It
focuses on the functional characteristics of grid cells such as the influence
of external cues or the alignment to environmental geometry, but also provides
a basic overview of the underlying neural substrate.
  Developed in the spirit of Lehnert et al. [24], our discussion aims to
illustrate the relationship between the statistical properties of grid cell
fires and the environmental geometry. Building on the idea of a simple
non-parametric test [24], we show how inference on grid cell hyperparameters
can be used to evaluate the significance of alignment between grid cells and
external cues. We further discuss how this approach can be extended to
incorporate other features such as the alignment between grid cells in the
same environment.
  Our code is freely available and can be used to provide an intuitive and
visual understanding of the relationship between grid cell fire statistics
and external geometry. It can also be used to provide an example framework for
analyzing grid cell data.
  In conclusion, we provide a practical guide on using statistical
approaches to analyse grid cell data and illustrate how they can be used to
address fundamental questions in the field of spatial cognition.

different regimes of differential rotation can be characterized with the Rossby
number. In particular, anti-solar differential rotation (fast poles, slow
equator) may exist for high Rossby number (slow rotators). If this regime

the atmosphere of Venus, and
modulation of its composition by interior-exterior cycling. The formation and
evolution of Venus's atmosphere, leading to contemporary surface conditions,
remain hotly debated topics, and involve questions that tie into many
disciplines. We explore these various inter-related mechanisms which shaped the
evolution of the atmosphere, starting with the volatile sources and sinks.
Going from the deep interior to the top of the atmosphere, we describe volcanic
outgassing, surface atmosphere interactions, and atmosphere escape.
Furthermore, we address more complex aspects of the history of Venus, including
the role of Late Accretion impacts, how magnetic field generation is tied into
long-term evolution, and the implications of geochemical and geodynamical
feedback cycles for atmospheric evolution. We highlight plausible end-member
evolutionary pathways that Venus could have followed, from accretion to its
present-day state, based on modeling and observations. In a first scenario, the
planet was desiccated by atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase. In a
second scenario, Venus could have harbored surface liquid water for long
periods of time, until its temperate climate was destabilized and it entered a
runaway greenhouse phase. In a third scenario, Venus's inefficient outgassing
could have kept water inside the planet, where hydrogen was trapped in the core
and the mantle was oxidized. We discuss differences and similarities between
these scenarios and other planetary bodies, and highlight the uniqueness of
Venus's evolutionary pathway. Finally, we address the implications of long-term
evolutionary scenarios for Venus' present-day and expected future
environment, and the implications of such scenarios for astrobiological
assessments of Venus.
  Venus's atmosphere is currently being transformed by atmospheric
dissipation. Over timescales of billions of years, the expected future changes
to the atmosphere are strongly dependent on the initial mass of volatiles in
Venus. We derive the long-lived timescales for this sequence of events, from
accretion to possible surface habitability and complete atmospheric
dissipation. We find that the timescales for atmospheric evolution on Venus are
only weakly dependent on the initial mass of volatiles under conditions of
high outgassing rates, such as those expected for a planet that experiences a
magma ocean phase. In these scenarios, the timescales for atmospheric
evolution are dominated by the timescales for magnetic field generation and
reversals.

plasma-based optical components which can sustain extremely high fields are
attracting increasing interest. Here, we propose a type of plasma waveplate

MacPherson gave a local and combinatorial formula for the
Pontrjagin classes of a differential manifold. We give an expanded version of
their discussion and highlight the origins of combinatorial differential
manifolds in their work.
  Combinatorial differential manifolds provide a link between smooth and
piecewise-linear manifolds. In particular, every smooth manifold has a
corresponding combinatorial differential manifold as a cover. With this in
mind, it is surprising that until now there was no direct connection between
Gelfand and MacPherson's formula and combinatorial differential manifolds. We
also use our expansion of Gelfand and MacPherson's discussion to clarify the
status of their formulation in relation to the generalization of Pontrjagin
classes to simplicial complexes given by Kirby and the second author.
  Finally, we give a computational version of Gelfand and MacPherson's
formulation. We do this by describing a natural chain complex whose reduced
Pontrjagin classes are given by Gelfand and MacPherson's formula. This provides
a completely explicit and computable version of their discussion.
  We relate our results to the work of Gilmer and Lutz on computing the
Pontrjagin classes of a smooth manifold using Gelfand and MacPherson's
formulation. Their computer program calculates these classes for the
simplicial complexes given by the barycentric subdivision of triangulations
of smooth closed manifolds. Our computational version of Gelfand and
MacPherson's formulation can also be used to simplify and extend their work.
  In a future work, we will show how our computational version of
Gelfand-MacPherson's formula will allow us to detect the genus of a virtual
moduli space of stable maps to a given target manifold.

framework to gain insight
into the dark matter structure formation. We investigate the impact of velocity
and density field information on the construction of halo mass function through
cosmological $N$-body simulations. In this direction, we train a Convolutional
Neural Network (CNN) on the initial snapshot of an only dark matter simulation
to predict the halo mass that individual particles fall into at $z=0$, in the
halo mass range of $10.5< \log(M / M_{\odot})<14$. Our results show a
negligible improvement from including the velocity in addition to the density
information when considering simulations based on the standard model of
cosmology ($\Lambda$CDM) with the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations
$A_s = 2\times10^{-9}$. In order to investigate the ellipsoidal collapse models
and to study the effect of velocity in smaller mass ranges, we increase the
initial power spectrum such that we see the effect of velocities in larger
halos which are in the resolution of our simulation. The CNN model trained on
the simulation snapshots with large $A_s$ shows a considerable improvement in
the halo mass prediction when adding the velocity field information.
Eventually, for the simulation with $A_s = 8 \times 10^{-8}$, the model trained
with only density information shows at least an order of improvement in the
halo mass prediction compared to the model without the velocity field. This
indicates that the velocity field has a considerable effect on the mass
formation of halos in simulations with high mass resolution.
  We also test the idea of using the smaller scale information in the input
images to the CNN to improve the halo mass formation. We train the CNN models
with different input image sizes to find that the highest accuracy is
achieved when the largest scales are included in the input image. This is
consistent with the statement that the largest halos are formed due to the
gravitational clustering of the large scale structure of the universe.
  In conclusion, by implementing a deep learning framework on the simulation
snapshots, we show that the velocity field has a considerable effect on the
mass formation of halos in simulations with high mass resolution.

of cosmology and the simulation parameters. In section. III we explain the
deep learning method and the features of the CNN model.

specifically on how the model is adapted to the data. In particular, we show

supervision and perform well in unsupervised setting, while CNNF models
requiring projection learning, such as Convolutive Nonnegative Convexex

propose a new unsupervised method, Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix
Factorization with Patch Learning, which obtains better results than the
unsupervised CNMF method mentioned above.

impossible to factor out non-stationary patterns.

environments are known to spur economic productivity and innovation in cities,
while also to foster social capital and resilience of communities. However,
mobility restrictions during the pandemic have forced people to substantially
reduce urban physical encounters, raising questions on the social implications
of such behavioral changes. In this paper, we study how the income diversity of
urban encounters have changed during different periods throughout the pandemic,
using a large-scale, privacy-enhanced mobility dataset of more than one million
anonymized mobile phone users in four large US cities, collected across three
years spanning before and during the pandemic. We find that the diversity of
urban encounters have substantially decreased (by 15% to 30%) during the
pandemic and has persisted through late 2021, even though aggregated mobility
metrics have recovered to pre-pandemic levels. Counterfactual analyses show
that while the reduction of outside activities (higher rates of staying at
home) was a major factor that contributed to decreased diversity in the early
stages of the pandemic, behavioral changes including lower willingness to
explore new places and changes in visitation preferences further worsened the
long-term diversity of encounters. Our findings suggest that the pandemic could
have long-lasting negative effects on urban income diversity, and provide
implications for managing the trade-off between the stringency of COVID-19
policies and the diversity of urban encounters as we move beyond the pandemic.

Moreover, the exposure over children and teenagers is similar to the one of the
whole population, while the exposure over schools and medical centers can be
lower than the one of the whole set of buildings. Finally, the exposure from 5G
is strongly lower than the pre-5G one when the building attenuation is
introduced and a maturity adoption level for 5G is assumed.
  From a regulatory point of view, our methodology can be applied over specific
situations, as the one of children standing in front a 5G cellular tower or a
school located at a specific distance from a 5G cellular tower. Moreover, our
approach can be extended to evaluate the exposure from 5G (and pre-5G) cellular
towers over other sensitive buildings, like hospitals and elderly homes.
Finally, the evaluation of the exposure from 5G (and pre-5G) cellular towers
over young people and buildings should be done by the regulators at each
national state, considering the specific antenna norms and standards defined
in each region.
  The main advantages of the proposed methodology are that it is simple to be
applied by regulators, standardization bodies and scientists. It does not
require a high computational effort and it is generally valid for all types
of 5G antennas. It can be used to evaluate the exposure from 5G (and pre-5G)
cellular towers over children, teenagers and sensitive buildings, as the school
and medical center. Moreover, the methodology can be extended to evaluate the
exposure from other types of 5G access points, as the ones based on Fixed
Point Access (FPA) and Fixed Wireless Access Point (FWAP).

the navigation of a dynamic indoor environment with a mobile platform with a

can operate in conditions such as rain, fog, dust, or dirt. The different
control layers, such as collision avoidance and corridor following behavior,

navigational outcome based on a zoning system around the mobile platform.

platform with one, two, or three sonar sensors in real time with 2D navigation.

experiments to demonstrate that the modular approach for the controller and
sensor fusion works optimally. The results of this work show stable and safe
navigation of indoor environments with dynamic objects.

Gaussian random field manifolds using the first and second fundamental forms

simulate the dynamics of these random fields and compute the Gaussian curvature

transitions. During the simulation, we have observed an unexpected phenomenon
that we called the \emph{curvature effect}, which indicates that a highly
asymmetric geometric deformation happens in the underlying parametric space
when there are significant increase/decrease in the system's entropy. This
asymmetric pattern relates to the emergence of hysteresis, leading to an
intrinsic arrow of time along the dynamics.

non-compact energy spectrum, what indicates that the presence of hysteresis is
a necessary condition for the birth of complex dynamics. In addition, we
analyze the connection between the entropy and the structural changes in the
system, indicating that the entropy itself is not the responsible for the
geometric transformation of the parametric space, but rather the changes in the

time, proposing that the underlying random field structure is the cause of the
arrow of time in these systems.

birth of complex behavior.

Variables (CV), known as asynchronous
polars, are still relatively poorly understood. An asynchronous polar is a
polar in which the spin period of the white dwarf is either shorter or longer
than the binary orbital period (typically within a few percent). The
asynchronous polars have been disproportionately detected in soft gamma-ray
observations, leading us to consider the possibility that they have
intrinsically harder X-ray spectra. We compared standard and asynchronous
polars in order to examine the relationship between a CV's synchronization
status and its spectral shape. Using the entire sample of asynchronous polars,
we find that the asynchronous polars may, indeed, have harder spectra, but that
the result is not statistically significant.
  A similar investigation of the relationship between spectral hardness and
average mass transfer rate also yields a possibly significant result: lower
mass transfer rates are correlated with harder spectra.
  Finally, we consider a simple model in which the mass transfer rate in non
conserving binary is correlated with the fractional spin-orbit lag in the
asynchronous binaries, leading to the possibly significant hardening of the
spectra of asynchronous polars compared to standards.
  Future observations, particularly of the highest mass transfer rate asynchronous
polars, are needed to fully understand this phenomenon.

metrology. Here, we propose an Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry to
sensitively detect the very weak local magnetic field, which is expelled by the
superconductor (as the "testing magnet") due to the Meissner effect. The
induced magnetic field gradient near the superconductor provides a centripetal

detected by using the atomic interferences. Given gravity acceleration of the
atoms have been measured at the accuracy of $10^{-12}$ g, the measured
sensitivity of the expelled local field could reach $10^{-14}$ T.

the superconductor. We discuss that this measurement sensitivity can be
improved by choosing suitable atomic states and cooling the atoms.

to expel the magnetic fields, not limited to the superconductor. This could
expand the application of measuring the hidden field expelled by the
superconductors, and also could provide the evidence of the different properties
of these materials.

the intra-cluster medium provide a
wealth of information on the dynamics of clusters of galaxies. The global
equilibrium of the ICM is believed to be partially ensured by non-thermal
pressure support, notably the dissipation of energy through turbulent motions.
Accurate mapping of turbulence using X-ray emission lines is challenging due to
the lack of spatially-resolved spectroscopy. Only future instruments such as
the X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU) on Athena will have the spatial and
spectral resolution to quantitatively investigate the ICM turbulence at all
scales. Powerful diagnostics for these studies are line shift and the line
broadening maps, and the second-order structure function. When estimating these
quantities, instruments will be limited by uncertainties of their measurements,
and by the sample variance (aka cosmic variance) of the observation. We extend
here the formalism started in our companion paper I to include the effect of
statistical uncertainties in the estimation of these line diagnostics, in
particular for structure functions. We demonstrate that statistics contribute
to the total variance through different terms, which depend on the geometry of
the detector, the spatial binning and the nature of the turbulent field. These
terms are important when probing the small scales of the turbulence. An
application of these equations is performed for the X-IFU, using synthetic
turbulent velocity maps of a Coma-like cluster. We show that even for fairly
realistic exposures, the statistics contribute significantly to the total
variance, especially at large spatial scales.
  We discuss the implications of these results for future observations with
X-IFU. We demonstrate that increasing the exposure time beyond what is
technologically required (to lower the phonon noise) is crucial to properly
probe the turbulence at all scales. We also show that the spatial binning
selected for the observation has a minor impact on the variance. Finally, we
show that even with moderate exposures, the statistics will dominate the
variance at cluster scales when using structure functions as turbulence
diagnostics, and will limit the proportion of clusters for which we will be able
to properly map their turbulence.
  Last, we propose a method to correctly estimate the statistics of these
line diagnostics in real observations. It consists in applying the same
processing to a mock sample of observations before adding the observation to the
real sample for the estimation of the statistics. This method is simple,
efficient and does not require any implementation of new algorithms

white dwarfs, and neutron stars are
known to be stable for long times. However, the physical conditions inside the
stellar interiors that allow these states are still a matter of research. It
has been formally demonstrated that both purely toroidal and purely poloidal
magnetic fields develop instabilities at some point in the star. On the other
hand, numerical simulations have proved the stability of roughly axisymmetric
magnetic field configurations inside stably stratified stars. These
configurations consist of mutually stabilizing toroidal and poloidal components
in a twisted torus shape. Previous studies have proposed rough upper and lower
bounds on the ratio of the magnetic energy in the toroidal and poloidal
components of the magnetic field. With the purpose of mapping out the parameter
space under which such configurations remain stable, we used the Pencil Code to
perform 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulations of the evolution of the magnetic
field in non-rotating, non-degenerate stars in which viscosity is the only
dissipation mechanism, both for stars with a uniform (barotropic) and radially
increasing (stably stratified) specific entropy. Furthermore, we considered
different conditions regarding the degree of stable stratification and the
magnetic energy in each component, roughly confirming the previously suggested
stability boundaries for the magnetic field.
  A interesting result that emerges from the simulations is that as the
statistical measure of the complexity of the magnetic field, its entropy,
increases throughout the evolution of the magnetic field, which suggests that
its principle of maximum entropy (the Prigogine's first law of self-organization)
is a sufficient condition for the development of magnetic structures with
structure, such as the twisted torus shape observed. Finally, our results
further support the idea that the apsidal oscillations observed in many stars,
including the Sun, can be caused by the buildup and decay of magnetic structures
with the period of the cycle of the star.
  We conclude that both toroidal and poloidal magnetic field components are
necessary for the magnetic field to be in a state of marginal stability within
the stars considered.
  Finally, we suggest that the development of negative-norm magnetic
instabilities in stars depends on the ratio of the magnetic energy in the
toroidal and poloidal components of the magnetic field.
  Based on these results, we propose a new stability boundary for the magnetic
field in non-rotating, non-degenerate stars.

of life, but for pop
music, people still rely on textual search engines like Google. We propose Pied
piper, a meta search engine for music. It can search for music lyrics, song
metadata and song audio or a combination of any of these as the input query and
efficiently return the relevant results.
  We implemented Pied piper as a web application using flask and it consists of
the following modules:
  - A web interface for users to input their queries and view results.
- A indexer module that indexes song audio, lyrics and metadata.
- A search module that uses the index and performs search based on the input
query and returns relevant results.
- A utility module that contains utility functions such as a function to
extract lyrics from web pages.
  We used the following algorithms in Pied piper:
  - For search, we used the BitTorrent DHT algorithm to create a distributed
hash table for indexing and searching. This allows us to efficiently search for
the required data from the index.
- We used the Google Speech recognition API to search for audio related to the
query.
- We used the Natural Language Processing library, spaCy, to search for
lyrics related to the query.
- We used the Music Information Retrieval library, madmom, to search for music
metadata related to the query.
  This is the first version of Pied piper and there is a lot of scope for
improvement. We plan to improve the index by using a more efficient data
structure and also by indexing more features. We plan to add more features to
the utility module and also more algorithms to the search module. For example,
we can add a feature to extract lyrics from large datasets like Wikipedia and
also add another algorithm to use the deep learning model, MusicNN, to search
for music metadata.
  In summary, Pied piper is a fully functional meta search engine for music
and it has a lot of potential for growth and improvement.

been an unsolved question of high-energy astrophysics. One approach for solving
this puzzle is to correlate UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos, since neutrinos
are a direct probe of hadronic interactions of cosmic rays and are not
deflected by magnetic fields. In this paper, we present three different
approaches for correlating the arrival directions of neutrinos with the arrival
directions of UHECRs. The neutrino data is provided by the IceCube Neutrino
Observatory and ANTARES, while the UHECR data with energies above $\sim$50 EeV
is provided by the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array. All
experiments provide increased statistics and improved reconstructions with
respect to our previous results reported in 2015. The first analysis uses a
high-statistics neutrino sample optimized for point-source searches to search
for excesses of neutrinos clustering in the vicinity of UHECR directions. The
second analysis searches for an excess of UHECRs in the direction of the
highest-energy neutrinos. The third analysis searches for an excess of pairs of
UHECRs and highest-energy neutrinos on different angular scales. None of the
analyses has found a significant excess, and previously reported
over-fluctuations are reduced in significance. Based on these results, we
update the confidence levels for the hypothesis that the UHECRs measured by
ground-based experiments are caused by heavy, relativistic topological
defect particles, which stabilize neutrino-point-source correlations. The
results range from $2.4$% to $3.5$%, depending on the energy range and the
assuming mass of the cosmic ray particles.

also update the expected sensitivity for detecting a neutrino point source
with an excess of UHECRs by a factor of $2-3$, corresponding to $10^2$
additional UHECRs within $0.5^\circ$ of a neutrino direction.

self-contact but also secondary branches of mixed modes and circumferentially
localized folds as a function of the rotation rate and the externally imposed
pressure. Both reflection-symmetric and symmetry-broken chiral states are
computed. The results are presented in the form of bifurcation diagrams. The
ratio of system scale to the natural length scale is found to determine the

as the solution profiles and onset of secondary bifurcations.

simulations of the full nonlinear problem. We show that the primary and
secondary branches computed in the weakly nonlinear analysis above are also
stable to relatively large perturbations and provide evidence for the
validity of the underlying asymptotic theory by comparing simulation finger
scales to the theoretically predicted ones. We also provide evidence for the
existence of a transient, strongly nonlinear regime which precededing the
onset of wave-like dynamics in each perturbation. A comparison of the onset of
chimera states in both the inextensible and extensible cell to that of a
coupled oscillator system is also provided.

vesicles. Finally, the strong similarity between the rotating Hele-Shaw cell
and the Earth's mantle during polar wind suggests that the mechanisms
demonstrated here may also be relevant to the formation of poloidal flux

  Grid computing in the mid-1990s seemed poised to revolutionize high-performance
computing. However, its wide adoption was hindered by technical complexities and
high start-up costs. To revive flagging investment interest, David Abramson and
Sajita Parashar reframed grid computing as translational computer science in
2000. This new framing helped reinvigorate investment and interest in grid
computing. However, the grid computing infrastructure that was developed in the
US was not widely adopted. It was the open source and collaboratively developed
Globus Toolkit that ultimately found widespread use in grid computing. To
understand its wide adoption, we apply the lens of translational computer
science to the development of the Globus Toolkit. We find that the Toolkit's
development followed a path that is consistent with the principles of
translational computer science. These principles may have contributed to the
Toolkit's success and widespread adoption.

trajectory of unoccupied RVs sequentially. To validate the effectiveness of the

autoscoring models, despite getting trained as "end-to-end" models with rich
contextual embeddings such as BERT, behave like bag-of-words models. A few
words determine the essay score without the requirement of any context making

studies on pre-trained representation learning models, which show that rich
linguistic features such as parts-of-speech and morphology are encoded by them.
Further, we also find that the models have learnt dataset biases, making them
oversensitive. To get better essay scoring mechanisms, we propose simple data
augmentation based tricks to make the models both stable and sensitive at the

carried out. Characterization of plasma parameters (i.e. electron temperature,
density, and plasma potential) followed by the implementation of a global model
of particle and power balance has been made. The existence of helicon mode
confirmed at lower magnetic fields (B <35 mT). To get the highest possible
plasma density, the optimization of the plasma source is presented to reach
helicon mode at the highest available magnetic field.

plasma potential, and the characterization of the sheath around the antenna.

this source at lower magnetic fields. The characterization of the plasma
environment will also help to understand the behavior of ICRF wave and plasma

cancer diagnosis, but it is
labor-intensive, in which tasks such as cell detection, classification, and
counting are particularly prominent. A common solution for automating these
tasks is using nucleus segmentation technology. However, it is hard to train a
robust nucleus segmentation model, due to several challenging problems, the
nucleus adhesion, stacking, and excessive fusion with the background. Recently,
some researchers proposed a series of automatic nucleus segmentation methods
based on point annotation, which can significant improve the model performance.
Nevertheless, the point annotation needs to be marked by experienced
pathologists. In order to take advantage of segmentation methods based on point
annotation, further alleviate the manual workload, and make cancer diagnosis
more efficient and accurate, it is necessary to develop an automatic nucleus
detection algorithm, which can automatically and efficiently locate the
position of the nucleus in the pathological image and extract valuable
information for pathologists. In this paper, we propose a W-shaped network for
automatic nucleus detection. Different from the traditional U-Net based method,
mapping the original pathology image to the target mask directly, our proposed
method split the detection task into two sub-tasks. The first sub-task maps the
original pathology image to the binary mask, then the binary mask is mapped to
the density mask in the second sub-task. After the task is split, the task's
difficulty is significantly reduced, and the model's performance is improved.
Specifically, the density mask is used to indicate the possible position of the
nucleus from the perspective of density, which can provide more detailed
information for the original binary mask. To evaluate the effectiveness of the
proposed method, we use 19,541 images from four public pathological image
datasets. The experimental results show that our proposed method is superior to
the U-Net based method. Our code and data are available at
https://github.com/ChenXiang143/NucleusDetection.

  This article describes our type-based static verification tool HELMHOLTZ for
Michelson, which is a statically typed stack-based language for writing smart
contracts that are executed on the blockchain platform Tezos. HELMHOLTZ is
designed on top of our extension of Michelson's type system with refinement
types. HELMHOLTZ takes a Michelson program annotated with a user-defined
specification written in the form of a refinement type as input; it then
typechecks the program against the specification based on the refinement type
system, discharging the generated verification conditions with the SMT solver
Z3. We briefly introduce our refinement type system for the core calculus
Mini-Michelson of Michelson, which incorporates the characteristic features
such as compound datatypes (e.g., lists and pairs), higher-order functions, and
invocation of another contract. \HELMHOLTZ{} successfully verifies several
practical Michelson programs, including one that transfers money to an account
and that checks a digital signature.

describe the underlying calculus and type system, while focusing on a
implementation of a verifier for a extended version of the calculus. This
article focuses on Michelson itself and how HELMHOLTZ is designed to work with

supersymmetric Yang-Mills theories with algebra
$\mathfrak{so}(4N)$ and appropriate choices of global structure can have
non-invertible symmetries. We identify the branes holographically dual to the
non-invertible symmetries, and derive the fusion rules for the symmetries from
the worldvolume dynamics on the branes.
  We also identify the extra states needed to realize the fusion rules as
coherent states constructed from twisted field configurations of harmonic
functions.
  Finally, we relate the harmonic function configurations to magnetic charges,
and derive the $\mathfrak{so}(4N)$ generalization of the Dirichlet charge bracket
to describe the fusion rules for the magnetic charges.
  This provides a purely mathematical derivation of the Dirichlet charge bracket
in the $\mathfrak{so}(4N)$ case, boosting the existing physical evidence.
Moreover, it shows that the non-invertible symmetries of $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric
Yang-Mills theories can be realized as D-branes wrapped on cycles of a manifold
with an appropriate fundamental group, thus giving a simple concrete example of
how D-branes can give rise to non-invertible symmetries.
Finally, we observe that our procedure to derive the Dirichlet charge bracket
works also for the algebra $\mathfrak{so}(4N+2)$, where it gives a slightly
different result. This suggests that there is a way to realize this algebra as
a subalgebra of a larger algebra with four-dimensional superconformal symmetry,

) and imperative algorithms
(pseudocodes) are two well-known coexisting concepts. Then what is their
relationship? Our answer is that
  \[ imperative\ algorithms\ =\ proofs\ with\ cuts \]
  This observation leads to a generalization to pseudocodes which we call {\it
logical pseudocodes}. It is similar to natural deduction proof of computability
logic\cite{Jap03,Jap08}. Each statement in it corresponds to a proof step in
natural deduction. Therefore, the merit over pseudocode is that each statement
is guaranteed to be correct and safe with respect to the initial
specifications. It can also be seen as an extension to computability logic web
(\colw) with forward reasoning capability.
  We demonstrate its usability by applying it to the proof of correctness of
the Euclid's algorithm for greatest common divisor. It is also observed to be
convenient for proving properties of numbers. Due to its similarity to natural
deduction, it is easy to use, especially for people who are familiar with it.
  Logical pseudocodes are executable too. Each proof step corresponds to a
transparent and guarenteed correct execution step, whether it is done by an
actual interpreter or by an idealized one in the mind.
  Finally, logical pseudocodes are reversible. Each reversible statement in it
guarantees the safe reversal. This is unusual for pseudocodes which are
typically non-reversible and, therefore, not suitable for undoing.
  The idea of proving (logical) pseudocodes by reflecting them into (natural
deduction) proofs leads to a generalization of computational proofs
(\comp) which can only be reflected backwards from proofs to pseudocodes. We
call a computational proof which can be reflected both ways (forward and
backward) {\it fully computational}. In a fully computational proof, each
computation (pseudocode) is guaranteed to be correct and safe with respect to
the initial specifications, in contrast to regular computational proofs which
only guarantee the correctness of the final answer but not the intermediate
computation. This is similar to the difference between our observation that
imperative algorithms are proofs with cuts and regular computational proofs.
  We demonstrate the utility of fully computational proofs by applying it to
the proof of solvability of the halting problem. It leads to an interesting
variation of Turing's argument and challenges the traditional understanding of
computability logic.

achieving extremely high data rates in next-generation wireless networks. While
the THz communication is conventionally envisioned for short-range wireless
applications due to the high atmospheric absorption at THz frequencies,
multi-hop directional transmissions can be enabled to extend the communication
range. However, to realize multi-hop THz communications, conventional beam
training schemes, such as exhaustive search or hierarchical methods with a
fixed number of training levels, can lead to a very large time overhead. To
address this challenge, in this paper, a novel hierarchical beam training
scheme with dynamic training levels is proposed to optimize the performance of
multi-hop THz links. In fact, an optimization problem is formulated to maximize
the overall spectral efficiency of the multi-hop THz link by dynamically and
jointly selecting the number of beam training levels across all the constituent
single-hop links. To solve this problem in presence of unknown channel state
information, noise, and path loss, a new reinforcement learning solution based
on the multi-armed bandit (MAB) is developed. Simulation results show the fast
convergence of the proposed scheme in presence of random channels and noise.
The results also show that the proposed scheme can yield up to 75% performance
gain, in terms of spectral efficiency, compared to the conventional
hierarchical beam training with a fixed number of training levels.
Moreover, the results reveal that the proposed scheme can reduce the beam
training time by about 50% compared to the exhaustive search beam training.
Finally, the results show that the proposed scheme can achieve 98% fairness
among the constituent single-hop links.
  \textbf{Significance---}The proposed novel hierarchical beam training with
dynamic training levels is significant for multi-hop THz communications to
optimally use the available time for beam training and data transmission in
presence of high noise and interference. The proposed scheme is also
significantly different from the related works as it uses a MAB-based
algorithmic approach to jointly optimize the beam training levels across all the
constituent single-hop links, which is not seen before in any of the related
works.

scattering screens, most of
unknown origin. Scintillation studies of pulsars provides a sensitive tool for
resolving these scattering screens and a means of measuring their properties.
In this paper, we report our analysis of 34 years of Arecibo observations of
PSR B1133+16, from which we have obtained high-quality dynamic spectra and
their associated scintillation arcs, arising from the scattering screens
located along the line of sight to the pulsar. We have identified six
individual scattering screens that are responsible for the observed
scintillation arcs, which persist for decades. Using the assumption that the
scattering screens have not changed significantly in this time, we have modeled
the variations in arc curvature throughout the Earth's orbit and extracted
information about the placement, orientation, and velocity of five of the six
screens, with the highest-precision distance measurement placing a screen at
just $5.46^{+0.54}_{-0.59}$ pc from the Earth. We associate the more distant of
these screens with an under-dense region of the Local Bubble.
  We find that the scattering screens are clustered in three regions along the
line of sight towards PSR B1133+16, with one of these regions coinciding with
the spiral arm intersection region near the Sun. Five of the six screens are
oriented approximately perpendicularly to the direction of the Galactic
center, a result consistent with previous studies of scattering screens. We
demonstrate that the orientation of the arms as seen by the Earth is
described by a spiral density wave with a pattern speed of $39.0^{+0.7}_{-0.6}$
km s$^{-1}$, consistent with previous spiral density wave studies, and show
that the scintillation arcs provide a sensitive probe of the arm structure.
Finally, we discuss the relationship between the scattering screens and the
visible spiral arms and propose that the screens represent the underlying
density fluctuations that give rise to the visible arms.
  We recommend that future observations of pulsars with long observation spans
and high timing precision be used to study the long-timescale scintillation
variations of a large number of pulsars in order to thoroughly map the
interstellar medium.

Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) is proposed to improve the limited pitch
controllability of vanilla WaveNet (WN) using pitch-dependent dilated
convolution neural networks (PDCNNs). Specifically, as a probabilistic
autoregressive generation model with stacked dilated convolution layers, WN
achieves high-fidelity audio waveform generation. However, the pure-data-driven
nature and the lack of prior knowledge of audio signals degrade the pitch
controllability of WN. For instance, it is difficult for WN to precisely
generate the periodic components of audio signals when the given auxiliary
fundamental frequency ($F_{0}$) features are outside the $F_{0}$ range observed
in the training data. To address this problem, QPNet with two novel designs is
proposed. First, the PDCNN component is applied to dynamically change the
network architecture of WN according to the given auxiliary $F_{0}$ features.
Second, a cascaded network structure is utilized to simultaneously model the
long- and short-term dependencies of quasi-periodic signals such as speech. The
performances of single-tone sinusoid and speech generations are evaluated. The
experimental results show the effectiveness of the PDCNNs for unseen auxiliary
$F_{0}$ features and the effectiveness of the cascaded structure for speech
generation.

of THH of a bicategory and shadows on that bicategory. As an application we

an object to its THH is the shadow of the monoidal category. Finally, we
prove that for a symmetric monoidal functor $F:\mathcal{C}\to \mathcal{D}$,

bicategories and prove that its THH is equivalent to the homotopy shadow
construction introduced by Lurie. This generalizes a result of Lurie for
effective homotopy shadow of a category.

  Sound source localization from video does not require explicit annotations
because mouth positions are generally easy to detect. Therefore, this task has
attracted considerable attention in recent years. Most existing works simply
train oral action recognition models to localize mouth parts and assume that the
sound source is the object whose mouth is closest to the optical center of the
video. Today, industrial-level annotations for objects in videos are extremely
expensive. Therefore, we ask the question: can we also recognize the identity
of the object emitting the sound without manual annotations? In other words,
assume that the model for localizing mouth parts is provided, the present
paper investigates how to prepare an model for recognizing objects for sound
sources. We show that, by simply adding auxiliary classification layers of an
appropriate depth, the feature map provided by a mouth action recognition
model can be turned into an object recognition model for sound sources. Our
theoretical analysis shows that such auxiliary classification layers can be viewed
as an information bottleneck that discriminatively learns to extract an
object representation from the mouth representation. As a result, the bottom
layers learn to generate mouth features that are complementary to the object
classification labels. The proposed method is trained solely from raw image
annotations of a benchmark dataset and no additional annotations are required.

element for TSS. Two different procedures are developed that allow the
visualization of the TSS effect: In the first one, we apply a coherent pump of

placing the system in contact with a phonon squeezed bath. Our model and
procedures show that in optomechanical systems TSS can be achieved with a high
fidelity.

measuring the optical coherences after the phonon cooling in two different
scenarios: When the optomechanical interaction is switched on and off, and in
the constant interaction mode. Our detection methods are applicable in different
optomechanical schemes, and they are especially useful in cases where the TSS
cannot be visualized by typical methods.
  We investigate two different optomechanical schemes: In the first one, a
rotating wave approximation (RWA) is applicable, and in the second scheme, the
full model (without RWA) is used. Our results show that in both schemes it is
possible to achieve TSS, but in different conditions.
  Finally, we show that the TSS effect can be assisted by a laser coil in the
case when the optomechanical interaction is not sufficient to achieve TSS. This
assistance procedure is also possible in the two different scenarios: With and
without constant optomechanical interaction.
  Our schemes and procedures present that the TSS effect can be achieved in
different optomechanical systems. Moreover, the TSS assisted by a laser coil
present an extra flexibility to be observed and detected.
  We hope that our results can be applied in different hybrid systems, and may
help to establish new procedures to transfer the squeezed states in the
mechanical part to an optical cavity.

different problems, for instance, to improve the precision of optical

incoming plane wavelet; \emph{iii)} reconstruction of the time-harmonic
solution from the time-domain solution via a Fourier transform in time. An
essential ingredient of the new method is a front-tracking mesh adaptation
algorithm for solving the problem in \emph{ii)}. By exploiting the limited
support of the wave front, this allows us to make the number of the required
degrees of freedom to reach a given accuracy significantly less dependent on
the frequency $\omega$. We also present a new algorithm for computing the
Fourier transform in \emph{iii)} that exploits the reduced number of degrees of
freedom corresponding to the adapted meshes. Numerical examples demonstrate the
advantages of the proposed method and the fact that the method can also be
applied with external source terms such as point sources and sound-soft

of translating speech in one language
into text in another language. Traditional cascaded approaches for ST, using
Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Machine Translation (MT) systems, are
prone to error propagation. End-to-end approaches use only one system to avoid
propagating error, yet are difficult to employ due to data scarcity. We explore
zero-shot translation, which enables translating a pair of languages that is
unseen during training, thus avoid the use of end-to-end ST data. Zero-shot
translation has been shown to work for multilingual machine translation, yet
has not been studied for speech translation. We attempt to build zero-shot ST
models that are trained only on ASR and MT tasks but can do ST task during
inference. The challenge is that the representation of text and audio is
significantly different, thus the models learn ASR and MT tasks in different
ways, making it non-trivial to perform zero-shot. These models tend to output
the wrong language when performing zero-shot ST. We tackle the issues by
including additional training data and an auxiliary loss function that
minimizes the text-audio difference. Our experiment results and analysis show
that the methods are promising for zero-shot ST. Moreover, our methods are
particularly useful in the few-shot settings where a limited amount of ST data
is available, with improvements of up to +11.8 BLEU scores.

experiments.

We make a direct comparison with the widely used $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only
model, depending on electronic filling. We consider all electron fillings of
the $d$-shell and compute the total magnetic moment, the spin, the occupancy of
each orbital, and the effective spin-orbit coupling strength (renormalized
through interaction effects) in terms of the bare interaction parameters,
spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting, focusing on the parameter
ranges relevant to 4d and 5d transition metal oxides. In various limits we
provide perturbative results consistent with our numerical calculations. We
find that the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be large, with up to 20\% occupation of
orbitals that are nominally "empty", which has experimental implications for
the interpretation of the branching ratio in experiments, and can impact the
effective local moment Hamiltonian used to study magnetic phases and magnetic
excitations in transition metal oxides. Our results can aid the theoretical
interpretation of experiments on these materials, which often fall in a regime
of intermediate coupling with respect to electron-electron interactions.
Furthermore, the effective spin-orbit coupling can change signs with increasing
electronic filling, which can have implications for understanding spin-orbit
controlled magnetic phase transitions in these materials. We provide a summary
of our results in terms of a set of rules applicable to different electron
fillings and interaction strengths.

interpretation of branch ratio measurements, which are often used to estimate

effective local moment Hamiltonian used to study magnetic phases and magnetic

mapping out the phase diagrams of these materials. Finally, our work provides a
template for understanding interaction-induced mixing between $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$
states in crystalline electronic fields that are lower symmetric than cubic,
which is common in many transition metal oxides.

require discretization by unstructured meshes, over which the direct evaluation
of the potential by quadrature becomes costly. In this paper, we present a
simple and efficient high-order algorithm for computing Newtonian potentials,
based on the use of Green's third identity for transforming the volume integral
into a collection of boundary integrals, which can be easily handled by the
Helsing-Ojala method. As a result, the time cost of the classically expensive
near field and self-interaction computations over an unstructured mesh becomes
roughly the same as the time cost of the FMM-based far field interaction
computation. One of the key components of our algorithm is the high-order 2-D
monomial approximation of a function over a mesh element, which is often
regarded as an ill-conditioned problem, since it involves the solution of a
Vandermonde linear system. In fact, it has long been observed that, when the
function is sufficiently smooth, and when a backward stable linear system

uniformly to high accuracy. We rigorously formalize this observation in this
paper. The performance of our algorithm is illustrated through several
numerical experiments.
